Computers store numbers in bits: tiny switches that are either zero or one.
For decades, the standard size for a whole number was thirty-two of them.
Thirty-two switches give about four point three billion combinations.
But programs need negative numbers too, so one switch is used for the sign.
That leaves thirty-one for the value. Set them all to one, and you get two billion, one hundred forty-seven million, four hundred eighty-three thousand, six hundred forty-seven.
It works like an old car odometer with every digit at nine.
Add one more, and everything rolls over.

Many computers keep time by counting the seconds since the first of January nineteen seventy.
It's called Unix time, and for decades it was stored in a signed thirty-two-bit number.

The fix is the one YouTube used: store time in sixty-four bits.
That lasts about two hundred ninety-two billion years.
Most modern phones and laptops already made the switch.
The risk is in older and embedded systems: machines built to run for decades, that are hard to update.
Engineers have a little over eleven years to find them.
Every one of these stories started the same way.
Someone picked a size for a number, and it seemed impossibly big.
Two billion views. Eight months without a reboot. A share worth four hundred thousand dollars.
The number didn't change. The world grew into it.
So when someone says we'll never count that high, remember: eventually, something does.
